challenges.title: Port Scan Stories
challenges.description:
A 30-second capture from a small office network. Somebody scanned one host, found one open port, and immediately closed the connection.

**Goal:** find the open port and the service banner sent after the handshake. The flag is in the banner.

hints.text: Filter `tcp.flags.syn == 1 && tcp.flags.ack == 0` to see the scan attempts.
The one port that answered with SYN/ACK is the one you want. Follow its stream.

challenges.title: Follow the Stream
challenges.description:
A developer swears the API only accepts encrypted traffic. The capture says otherwise — one request went out over plain HTTP, including a header that should never have left the machine.

**Goal:** reconstruct the request and read the flag from the custom header.

hints.text: Filter `http.request` and follow the TCP stream.
Look at `X-Debug-Token`. Production would never send that.

challenges.title: DNS Tunneling 101
challenges.description:
The firewall allows DNS because DNS is always allowed. A workstation has been making a lot of very long queries to one domain, each with a different subdomain.

**Goal:** extract the encoded chunks in query order, decode them, and rebuild the exfiltrated file.

hints.text: Filter `dns.qry.name contains "tunnel"`. Sort by frame time, not frame number.
The first label is base32, the second label is the sequence number in hex.

challenges.title: Covert Channel
challenges.description:
No TCP, no UDP, no DNS — just ICMP echo requests with suspiciously consistent payloads. Each request carries one byte of the message, XOR-ed with that packet's TTL.

**Goal:** rebuild the transmitted payload. The first sixteen packets are a synchronisation header; the encoding is documented in the attached analyst note.

hints.text: Read the analyst note before writing a single line of code.
Payload bytes are XOR-ed with the TTL field. The first 16 packets are a sync header you can discard.
